title: The un-ordered UN order – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Mark Leonard argues the world has moved beyond disorder into 'un-order', where states act without any common framework, illustrated by the US-Israel war on Iran and the weaponised closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Multilateralism is migrating to improvised middle-power initiatives, and Europe should act as 'artisan' rather than 'architect' — notably by convening a coalition to keep food and fertiliser moving amid a looming global food crisis.

insights.claim: The international order is in worse shape than at any point since 1945: China and Russia never fully accepted it, assertive middle powers resent it, and its principal financial backer — the American public — has lost interest in underwriting it.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Loss of the US as funder and guarantor removes the backstop for global public goods, raising structural geopolitical risk premia.
insights.quote: its principal financial backer, the American public, has lost interest in underwriting it
insights.locator: As world leaders descend on New York

insights.claim: No new order is forming: this is not an interregnum between US-led and China-led orders but 'un-order', a situation in which states act without reference to any common framework, distinct from past disorder where rule-breakers still recognised the framework.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Investors should not model a bipolar US-China transition; expect fragmented, ad hoc crisis dynamics with no shared rules to anchor outcomes.
insights.quote: I call it un-order: a situation in which states act without reference to any common framework.
insights.locator: Sadly, no new order is in the making.

insights.claim: After the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in February 2026, the parties could not even agree whether a ceasefire existed, let alone who had won.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Ambiguous conflict end-states mean Middle East energy risk cannot be priced off formal ceasefire announcements.
insights.quote: the parties could not even agree whether a ceasefire existed, let alone who had won
insights.locator: One can already see this new dispensation

insights.claim: Disputes now jump across domains, as when Trump's designs on Greenland led to tariff threats against the EU.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Territorial or security disputes can rapidly become trade shocks, raising cross-asset contagion risk for EU exporters.
insights.locator: One can already see this new dispensation

insights.claim: Over half of globally traded staple crops pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and now the Bab al-Mandab has shown what happens when these are used for leverage.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Simultaneous closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab hits both energy and food/fertiliser flows, supporting elevated freight, oil and grain prices.
insights.quote: Over half of globally traded staple crops pass through at least one maritime chokepoint
insights.locator: One can already see this new dispensation

insights.claim: Russia's war on Ukraine, the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz and the strongest El Niño on record are together threatening global food supplies when 2.3bn people already face food insecurity.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A compound supply shock points to rising agricultural commodity and fertiliser prices and food-driven inflation and instability in import-dependent emerging markets.
insights.quote: the strongest El Niño on record are threatening global food supplies at a time when 2.3bn people already face food insecurity

insights.claim: The UN helped tackle the 2022 food crisis but probably will be unable to play the same role this time.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Absence of a Black Sea Grain Initiative-style institutional fix implies a longer, less-managed food price shock.

insights.claim: Europe should convene a global coalition with Brazil, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Turkey to pool resources and negotiate practical arrangements keeping food and fertiliser shipments moving.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Watch for EU-led food/fertiliser corridor deals that could cap agricultural price spikes and benefit these exporter/transit states.

insights.claim: Multilateralism is not dying but migrating: ECFR research finds middle powers building creative new forms of cooperation that do what the UN was built to do, in a more improvised, ad hoc fashion.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Influence and deal flow are shifting to minilateral platforms and middle-power hubs, which become new nodes for capital and diplomacy.
insights.quote: it would be a mistake to think that multilateralism itself is dying. Instead, it is migrating and being transformed
insights.locator: Yet even in a world of un-order

insights.claim: Examples of the new multilateralism include Barbados's Bridgetown Initiative on climate and development finance, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and Lobito Corridor binding countries through infrastructure rather than treaties, and Qatar, Oman and Turkey as go-to mediators from Gaza to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Infrastructure corridors (IMEC, Lobito) are becoming geopolitical instruments, channelling investment flows to aligned states.

insights.claim: China has acted as an 'artisan', building up the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and an expanded BRICS, joining the Arctic Council as an observer, and writing surveillance-friendly preferences into ITU internet standards.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: China's standards-setting in telecom bodies shapes future tech markets and regulatory alignment in the Global South.
insights.locator: Europeans have responded to all this as architects

insights.claim: Europeans have acted as 'architects' — drawing blueprints and defending universal norms — while others act as 'artisans' who improvise and repurpose; Europe has the furthest to catch up but much to gain, with Canada's Mark Carney seeking an 'alliance for the future' with the EU as an anchor for the West.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: EU-Canada alignment signals the EU emerging as the hub of a post-US Western bloc, relevant for trade and defence partnerships.
insights.locator: For Europeans, this is an uncomfortable moment.

insights.claim: Europe should engage the new builders, including seeking observer status in groupings it treats as rivals and using the UN as connective tissue linking the Bridgetown Initiative to international financial institutions and Qatar's deal-making to legal and reconstruction bodies.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Possible EU engagement with BRICS/SCO-type formats would mark a significant shift in bloc alignment.
insights.locator: To fulfil this role, Europeans must do three things.

insights.claim: Europeans have eroded the credibility of the rule of law by defending it rhetorically but not in practice, and should instead enforce a narrower set of rules with buy-in beyond the West: prohibitions on territorial conquest, targeting civilians and nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A narrower, enforcement-focused EU stance could mean more consistent sanctions on territorial conquest but less norm-driven conditionality elsewhere.
insights.quote: they have spent the last few years eroding the credibility of the rule of law by defending it rhetorically but not in practice

insights.claim: With the Trump administration openly hostile to multilateralism and the UN about to choose a new secretary-general, it is unclear how much longer the system can stagger on.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: The secretary-general selection is a near-term marker of whether the UN retains relevance or erodes further.
insights.locator: As world leaders descend on New York
